title: Repairing Trust After Letting Someone Down
description: Your close friend Alex recently went through a difficult time — they were moving to a new apartment while dealing with a stressful period at work. Alex asked you weeks in advance if you could help them move on Saturday, and you agreed. But when Saturday came, you had completely forgotten — you had made other plans with another group of friends and didn't realize the conflict until Alex texted you that morning asking what time you'd arrive. You apologized briefly by text and said you couldn't make it. Alex responded, "It's fine," but you could tell it wasn't. It's been five days, and Alex hasn't reached out since. You've heard from a mutual friend that Alex ended up moving mostly alone. You feel like your earlier apology was inadequate, and you want to reach out again — but you're worried that another text apology might come across as hollow or just something you're doing to make yourself feel better. You want to send Alex a message.

title: Expressing Gratitude While Making a Difficult Request
description: Your close friend Jordan helped you get through a really difficult period a few months ago. When you were going through a rough time after a bad breakup, Jordan checked in on you almost every day, brought you food, and even rearranged their own schedule to spend time with you. You never properly thanked them for all of that — you kept meaning to but the moment never felt right, and now months have passed. Recently, you found out that Jordan has a connection at a company you're trying to get a job at. You'd really like to ask Jordan to put in a good word or introduce you, but you feel awkward asking for another favor when you haven't even properly acknowledged what they already did for you. You want to send Jordan a message.

title: Expressing Honest Concern Without Damaging the Friendship
description: Your close friend Riley has been dating someone new for about two months. You have met their partner a few times, and each time you noticed things that made you uneasy. In group settings, their partner often dismissed Riley's opinions or made subtle comments that put them down. Last week, Riley canceled plans with you at the last minute, saying their partner “didn’t want them going out.” Since starting this relationship, Riley has also seemed less like themselves — quieter, more apologetic, and less spontaneous than usual. You are not sure whether you are overinterpreting things, but you are genuinely worried about them. You want to say something, but you are afraid Riley might get defensive or feel judged. You want to send Riley a message.
